Starting Your Touring Journey

Your first touring bike should build confidence, not test it. New riders often make the mistake of buying too much motorcycle — a heavy, powerful machine that is intimidating in traffic and exhausting on twisty roads. The best beginner touring bikes are light, forgiving, and manageable while still being genuinely capable of carrying you and your luggage across the country.

What New Riders Need

  • Manageable weight — Under 200kg wet is ideal. Heavy bikes are tiring and intimidating for new riders, especially at low speeds and in car parks.
  • Smooth power delivery — Linear, predictable throttle response builds confidence. Aggressive, peaky engines can catch out inexperienced riders.
  • Low seat height — Being able to flat-foot the ground provides confidence at stops and in traffic. Most manufacturers offer lowering kits.
  • ABS — Non-negotiable. ABS prevents front wheel lockups under heavy braking, the most common cause of single-vehicle accidents for new riders.
  • Forgiving handling — Stable, neutral handling that does not punish small mistakes. Avoid aggressive sport bikes for touring.

Best Beginner Touring Bikes

Honda CB500X — The gold standard beginner tourer. A2 licence compliant with restriction, light at 199kg, comfortable upright riding position, and Honda's legendary reliability. The 471cc parallel twin is smooth and economical with enough power for motorway touring.

Kawasaki Versys-X 300 — An adventure-styled tourer with a low 815mm seat height. The 296cc twin is peppy enough for A-road touring and supremely economical. Light and flickable through bends.

Yamaha Tenere 700 — For new riders who passed their test on a full licence, the Tenere is manageable at 204kg with a confidence-inspiring chassis. The CP2 engine is torquey and forgiving. Outstanding on B-roads and capable off-road.

Suzuki V-Strom 650 — Slightly larger but still very manageable. The V-twin engine is smooth and unstressed, the chassis is stable and forgiving, and the fuel economy is excellent. A bike many riders keep for years.

Royal Enfield Himalayan 450 — The new Himalayan is purpose-built for adventure at a low price. Light weight, low seat, and a torquey single-cylinder engine. Ideal for riders who want to explore green lanes alongside tarmac roads.

Do not buy your dream touring bike as your first bike. Buy a bike you can learn on, tour on, and potentially drop without heartbreak. After 10,000 miles, you will know exactly what you want from your next machine.

Building Experience

Start with day rides to build confidence before attempting overnight tours. Gradually extend your distances as your skills and stamina improve. Join a local riding group to learn from experienced tourers — most clubs welcome new riders and will adjust pace to suit. keyTakeaways: A first touring bike should build confidence, so aim for under 200kg wet where possible.
The Honda CB500X is the gold-standard beginner tourer at 199kg and A2 compliant.
Low seat height and ABS are priorities for new riders at stops and under braking.
The Kawasaki Versys-X 300 has an accessible 815mm seat and lively 296cc twin.
Start with day rides and build distance gradually before overnight tours.

pros: Manageable weight and forgiving power build confidence quickly.
Most models offer lowering kits for shorter riders.
Strong resale means low cost of ownership while you learn.
cons: Smaller-capacity options feel stretched two-up on motorways.
You will likely outgrow the bike after around 10,000 miles.

faq.q: Do I need ABS as a new rider?
faq.a: ABS is effectively non-negotiable for beginners. It prevents front-wheel lockups under heavy braking, the most common cause of single-vehicle accidents for new riders. Every bike we recommend here is available with ABS, and it is worth insisting on when buying used.

faq.q: What seat height suits shorter beginners?
faq.a: The Kawasaki Versys-X 300 has a low 815mm seat that lets most riders flat-foot the ground. If you like a taller bike such as the Tenere 700 or Himalayan 450, most manufacturers offer lowering kits and low seat options to improve confidence at stops.

faq.q: Can I tour on an A2 licence?
faq.a: Yes. The Honda CB500X is A2 compliant with restriction and is genuinely capable of week-long touring. The 471cc twin is smooth and economical with enough power for motorways, and it is light at 199kg, so it never feels intimidating in traffic.

faq.q: Should I buy my dream bike first?
faq.a: No. Buy a bike you can learn on, tour on and potentially drop without heartbreak. After around 10,000 miles you will know exactly what you want from your next machine, and a heavy, powerful first bike often proves intimidating and exhausting on twisty British roads.
